native_result.query: How is the advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students related to Socioeconomic status levels?
native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students is more pronounced at lower SES levels with the interaction term for Socioeconomic status and being black having a coefficient of 0.7606
native_result.HypoB: In the NLSY79 data (1979 baseline; primary SES axis = total net family income, 1978, winsorized at the 99th percentile; complete-case N=10,071), Black students do NOT show a raw (unadjusted) advantage in educational attainment at any family-income level — they trail non-Black/non-Hispanic students in mean grade completed, in some-college attendance (grade>=13), and in the very few grade-16 (BA) counts, in every income stratum. What the data do show is that the Black-non-Black attainment gap is strongly dependent on SES level and NARROWS as SES rises: it is most pronounced at the lowest SES and smallest (near parity) at the highest SES. On the family-income axis the Black-non-Black gap is: mean grade completed -1.47 grade levels in the lowest income tertile (<$7,000), -0.70 in the middle ($7,000-$17,000), and -0.25 in the highest (>$17,000); some-college attendance -10.4 pp (low), -2.6 pp (mid), -2.5 pp (high). The race x income interaction is statistically significant (OLS +0.032 grade-levels per $1,000, p<.001; categorical joint Wald chi2=5.17, p=.006, with Black x mid +0.61, p=.011, and Black x high +0.71, p=.003, relative to the low-income stratum). The mechanism is that Black students' education is far more responsive to family income than non-Black students' (Black income-slope +0.032 grade-levels/$1,000, p<.001, versus ~0 for non-Black, p=.80): higher-income Black students 'catch up' to non-Black peers, so the penalty of being Black on 1979 attainment is concentrated at the bottom of the SES distribution. The relationship is therefore: the (conditional) Black-non-Black gap does NOT flip into an advantage at any SES level; it narrows monotonically with rising family income, is widest at the lowest SES, and is essentially closed (~0.25 grade level; ~2.5 pp) at the highest SES. On the robustness axis of parental education the pattern is less clean and partly reversed (mean-grade gap roughly flat at -0.54/-0.39/-0.52; on some-college Black students from low-education families are nominally slightly ahead, +1.3 pp, while the gap reverses to a Black disadvantage, -6.6 pp, at the highest parental-education level - Black x parental-education interaction negative, p=.03). On the 1996-wealth sensitivity axis (reverse-causal, 44% missing, flagged fragile) the income-style narrowing reappears but more weakly (gaps -0.53/-0.45/-0.39; interaction p=.06). Caveats: the literal 1979 BA (grade>=16) is too sparse to test directly (only 4 Black vs 20 non-Black in the complete case; Black never exceeds non-Black in any stratum), so the inference rests on the continuous-grade and some-college+ proxies; and the 1979 snapshot (respondents aged 14-22) captures early life-course attainment rather than final degree completion. Bottom line: the 'advantage in BA completion for Black students' is not a uniform rate advantage in this data; it is best characterized as Black students' attainment being unusually responsive to family income, so that the Black attainment disadvantage is concentrated at the lowest SES and is largely eroded - approaching parity with non-Black students - at the highest SES.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (N=12,686). Cleaned 'Highest grade completed, 1979' (DK code 95 -> missing; 152 missing). Defined outcomes: literal BA (grade>=16, descriptive), some-college+ (grade>=13), continuous grade. Primary SES = total net family income, PCY 1979, winsorized at p99 ($60k); complete-case (grade+income) N=10,071. Stratified into income tertiles (T1<$7k, T2<$17k, T3); computed Black vs non-Black (Hispanic secondary) stratum-specific gaps for mean grade, some-college %, and BA counts. Estimated race x SES interaction via OLS on grade, logit on some-college, and categorical logit race x tertile with joint Wald test. Robustness: parental-education index (mother+father grade 1979). Sensitivity: 1996 net wealth (flagged reverse-causal, 44% missing). Reported complete-case n and missingness-by-race throughout; winsorized top-coded income.

sub_hypo.text: Black students have no raw educational-attainment advantage over non-Black/non-Hispanic students in any family-income stratum, but their disadvantage narrows monotonically as family income rises.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 1979 baseline, respondents aged 14–22; complete cases for grade and income (N=10,071). Primary SES is 1978 total net family income recorded in 1979, winsorized at the 99th percentile ($60,000). Income strata are low (<$7,000), middle ($7,000–$17,000), and high (>$17,000). Grade code 95 is treated as missing. Outcomes reflect early attainment rather than final degree completion.
variables: Total net family income, previous calendar year, 1979
sub_hypo.relations: Black minus non-Black/non-Hispanic mean-grade gaps are -1.47, -0.70, and -0.25 grades across low, middle, and high income; some-college+ (grade>=13) gaps are -10.4, -2.6, and -2.5 percentage points. The disadvantage is greatest at low income and approaches parity at high income without becoming an advantage.

sub_hypo.text: Black students' educational attainment is more responsive to family income than non-Black/non-Hispanic students' attainment.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 1979 early-life attainment; grade-and-income complete-case N=10,071, using 1978 family income recorded in 1979 and winsorized at $60,000. Race-by-income interactions are assessed with OLS for grade and logistic models for some-college+, including categorical income-tertile interactions.
variables: Total net family income, previous calendar year, 1979
sub_hypo.relations: The OLS race-by-income interaction is +0.032 grade levels per $1,000 (p<.001). The Black income slope is +0.032 grades per $1,000 (p<.001), versus approximately zero for non-Black students (p=.80). Categorical interactions relative to low income are Black×middle +0.61 (p=.011) and Black×high +0.71 (p=.003), with reported joint Wald chi2=5.17 (p=.006).

sub_hypo.text: Literal BA-level attainment shows no Black advantage in any income stratum, but is too sparse for direct hypothesis testing.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 1979 baseline, ages 14–22; grade-and-income complete-case N=10,071, with family income winsorized at the 99th percentile. BA-level attainment is defined descriptively as grade>=16, not final degree completion.
variables: Total net family income, previous calendar year, 1979
sub_hypo.relations: Only 4 Black versus 20 non-Black students reach grade>=16 in the complete-case sample; Black counts never exceed non-Black counts within an income stratum. Consequently, inference relies on continuous grade and some-college+ proxies rather than direct BA testing.

sub_hypo.text: The income-based narrowing of the Black attainment disadvantage is not consistently reproduced using parental education; the some-college pattern partly reverses.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 robustness analysis of 1979 attainment using a parental-education index based on mother's and father's highest completed grades in 1979.
variables: Highest grade completed by respondent's mother, 1979
Highest grade completed by respondent's father, 1979
sub_hypo.relations: Black minus non-Black mean-grade gaps are roughly flat across low, middle, and high parental education (-0.54, -0.39, -0.52). For some-college+ (grade>=13), Black students have a nominal +1.3-percentage-point advantage at low parental education but a -6.6-point disadvantage at high parental education. The Black-by-parental-education interaction is negative (p=.03).

sub_hypo.text: Using 1996 family wealth as SES reproduces a weaker narrowing of the Black educational-attainment disadvantage.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 sensitivity analysis relating 1979 attainment to 1996 family net wealth; flagged as fragile because wealth is measured after attainment, raising reverse-causality concerns, and has 44% missingness.
sub_hypo.relations: Black minus non-Black mean-grade gaps narrow from -0.53 to -0.45 to -0.39 across increasing wealth strata; the race-by-wealth interaction has p=.06.
